_comment: Config subtrees replaced WHOLESALE on save instead of deep-merged.
These are all user-owned MAPS whose keys can be deleted (ui.customThemes,
claude.budgets, projects). A deep merge can only ever add or overwrite keys,
so under one a removed entry comes straight back — the caller therefore
sends the entire surviving map and the writer takes it as the whole truth.
This list used to be two hand-kept copies on the TypeScript side alone
(configService.saveConfig and the renderer's configPatch, which trims a save
down to what changed) and they drifted: `projects` was wholesale in one and
trimmed in the other, so saving one project's icon shipped a one-entry map
that main took as the whole truth — every other project lost its identity
(fixed 2026-08-14, commit c4963a73, unifying the TS side onto
apps/desktop/src/main/shared/configWholesale.ts).
That fix never reached the Go brain, which answers config.save for every
bus caller (web, mobile, and every MCP save_config call — an agent's writes
ALWAYS go through the brain, never the desktop's in-process path). The brain
hand-special-cased only ui.customThemes and claude.budgets, so a project
delete sent over MCP silently failed to delete: safe (nothing is lost), but
a real cross-language disagreement about what config.save clears. This
fixture is what keeps the next entry from drifting the same way again.
THE RULE for adding a path here: a value belongs on this list when it is a
user-owned map whose keys the user can individually delete, and 'the caller
resends everything they want kept' is how that delete is expressed. A plain
scalar or a map nobody deletes entries from does not belong here — it merges
normally.
WHAT A WHOLESALE VALUE MAY BE — the `valueCases` block below.
Replacing rather than merging makes the VALUE'S TYPE load-bearing, and the two
writers disagreed about it in opposite and equally wrong directions. The Go
brain coerced any non-object at one of these paths to an empty map:
if vMap, ok := v.(map[string]any); ok { dst[leaf] = vMap }
else                                  { dst[leaf] = map[string]any{} }
so one malformed save DELETED every project's label, colour, icon, favourite
flag, delivery mode, yolo flag and worktreeSetup hooks — and returned the
emptied config as a SUCCESSFUL save. Nothing is backed up on a successful write
(writeConfigYAML backs up only an UNPARSEABLE file), so there was nothing to
recover from. The TS writer took the same input and wrote it through verbatim
(dst[leaf] = src[leaf] ?? {}), leaving a string where a map belongs, so every
config.projects[cwd] lookup answered undefined.
It was reachable rather than exotic: an agent's config writes ALWAYS go through
the brain, and the MCP facade registered save_config as a bare free-form object
with no input schema, so a client that serialised its argument sent `projects`
as a STRING and was coerced instead of refused.
Both writers now REFUSE, write nothing, and say so. `null` is refused with the
rest: an empty object already spells 'empty this map', unambiguously and in
both languages, so null adds no expressive power and is far likelier to be an
accident (a serialiser's undefined, a lookup that missed) than an intent to
delete everything the user owns. An explicit JS `undefined` is NOT in this
corpus and is not a refusal: it is how JavaScript spells 'I did not provide
this', JSON cannot carry it, and the Go side therefore never sees it — the TS
loader pins that one separately.
THE BLOCK REGISTRY. Every array-of-objects block in this file must be declared
here and everything here must be a block — closure in both directions, so a new
block is a failure until someone says what its cases must carry, and a renamed
one cannot quietly stop being validated.
This fixture used to be on both vocabulary guards' no-blocks exemption list
(cmd/brain/corpusvocab_test.go vocabExempt, contractsVocabulary.test.ts
NO_BLOCK_FIXTURES) because it carried only the `paths` list. Adding valueCases
took it off both.

valueCases.why: applyWholesale over ONE dotted path, judging the VALUE the caller sent there: which values are taken as the new map, and which are refused with nothing written.

refusalReasons.not-an-object: The value at a wholesale path is present but is not a JSON object. Refused by BOTH writers with nothing written: coercing it to {} deletes the user's map and reports success, and writing it through verbatim leaves a non-map where every reader indexes a map.

valueCases.name: an object at projects IS the new map
valueCases.why: The whole point of a wholesale path: re-sending the surviving map is the only way to express a delete, and the survivor keeps every field it came with.

valueCases.name: an empty object at projects empties the map
valueCases.why: {} is the ONE unambiguous way to say 'empty this map'. It stays accepted, which is what lets null be refused without losing any expressive power.

valueCases.name: a JSON string at projects is refused, not coerced to an empty map
valueCases.why: THE LIVE DEFECT. An MCP client that serialised its save_config argument sent exactly this, and the brain answered by deleting every project and reporting success.

valueCases.name: null at projects is refused
valueCases.why: Both writers used to read null as 'empty it' ({} in Go, ?? {} in TS). {} already says that; a null at a wholesale path is a serialiser accident far more often than an intent to delete a user's whole map.

valueCases.name: an array at projects is refused
valueCases.why: An empty array is the shape a client gets from serialising an empty collection in a language where maps and lists share a literal. typeof [] === 'object' in JS, so the TS check has to exclude arrays explicitly or this one slips through as a map.

valueCases.name: a number at projects is refused
valueCases.why: 0 and false are the falsy scalars: a guard written as a truthiness test rather than a type test treats them differently from a non-empty string, so both are in the corpus.

valueCases.name: false at projects is refused
valueCases.why: The other falsy scalar. Pinned beside 0 for the same reason.

valueCases.name: a nested path takes an object: ui.customThemes
valueCases.why: A wholesale path with a parent segment must reach the leaf and replace it, not stop at the parent — the nested walk is a second implementation in each language.

valueCases.name: a string at a nested path is refused too: ui.customThemes
valueCases.why: The refusal must live at the leaf, not at the top level: a guard bolted onto the caller's top-level keys would miss every nested wholesale path.

valueCases.name: a nested path takes an object: claude.budgets
valueCases.why: The third wholesale path, exercised so the corpus covers every entry of `paths` rather than just the one the incident happened to hit.

valueCases.name: null at a nested path is refused: claude.budgets
valueCases.why: Budgets are per-model spend limits; silently emptying them turns every configured cap off while reporting a saved config.
